claim: Intermittent recordings provide brief 'snapshots' of task-related neural dynamics but fail to address how neural activity is modulated outside of task context and across a wide range of active and inactive behavioral states.
source: Such intermittent recordings provide brief 'snapshots' of task-related neural dynamics (Georgopoulos et al., 1986; Hanks et al., 2015; Murakami et al., 2014), but fail to address how neural activity is modulated outside of task context and across a wide range of active and inactive behavioral states, (for exceptions see [Ambrose et al., 2016; Evarts, 1964; Gulati et al., 2014; Hengen et al., 2016; Hirase et al., 2001; Lin et al., 2006; Mizuseki and Buzsáki, 2013; Santhanam et al., 2007; Wilson and McNaughton, 1994]).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work and represents established knowledge in the field about limitations of intermittent recordings.

claim: Intermittent recordings are ill-suited for reliably tracking the same neurons over time.
source: Furthermore, intermittent recordings are ill-suited for reliably tracking the same neurons over time (Dickey et al., 2009; Emondi et al., 2004; Fraser and Schwartz, 2012; McMahon et al., 2014a; Santhanam et al., 2007; Tolias et al., 2007)
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior studies demonstrating this limitation.

claim: Calcium imaging is unsuitable for continuous long-term recordings due to photobleaching, phototoxicity, cytotoxicity, and requirements for head-restraint.
source: While in vivo calcium imaging allows the same neuronal population to be recorded intermittently over long durations (Huber et al., 2012; Liberti et al., 2016; Peters et al., 2014; Rose et al., 2016; Ziv et al., 2013), photobleaching, phototoxicity, and cytotoxicity (Grienberger and Konnerth, 2012; Looger and Griesbeck, 2012), as well as the requirements for head-restraint in many versions of such experiments (Dombeck et al., 2007; Huber et al., 2012; Peters et al., 2014), make the method unsuitable for continuous long-term recordings.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work documenting these limitations of calcium imaging.

claim: Calcium imaging has relatively poor temporal resolution, limiting its ability to resolve precise spike patterns.
source: Calcium imaging also has relatively poor temporal resolution (Grienberger and Konnerth, 2012; Vogelstein et al., 2009), limiting its ability to resolve precise spike patterns (Vogelstein et al., 2010; Yaksi and Friedrich, 2006) (but see Gong et al., 2015 for an alternative high-speed voltage sensor).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies on calcium imaging temporal resolution.

claim: Extracellular recordings using electrode arrays can measure the activity of many single neurons simultaneously with sub-millisecond resolution.
source: In contrast, extracellular recordings using electrode arrays can measure the activity of many single neurons simultaneously with sub-millisecond resolution (Buzsáki, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior work and represents established knowledge about extracellular recording capabilities.

claim: A major reason continuous long-term electrical recordings are not routinely performed is the laborious and difficult process of reliably tracking single units from longitudinal datasets.
source: Despite the unique benefits of continuous (24/7) long-term electrical recordings, they are not routinely performed. A major reason is the inherently laborious and difficult process of reliably and efficiently tracking the activity of single units from such longitudinal datasets (Einevoll et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation and represents an inference about why continuous recordings are not common.

claim: Firing rates of individual neurons can vary over many orders of magnitude.
source: wherein firing rates of individual neurons can vary over many orders of magnitude (Hromádka et al., 2008; Mizuseki and Buzsáki, 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies documenting this variability.

claim: Spike waveforms change over time.
source: and spike waveforms change over time (Dickey et al., 2009; Emondi et al., 2004; Fraser and Schwartz, 2012; Okun et al., 2016; Santhanam et al., 2007; Tolias et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior studies demonstrating waveform drift.

claim: The authors developed an unsupervised spike-sorting algorithm that automatically processes raw data from electrode array recordings and clusters spiking events into putative single units, tracking their activity over long timescales.
source: To efficiently parse the large streams of neural data, we developed an unsupervised spike-sorting algorithm that automatically processes the raw data from electrode array recordings, and clusters spiking events into putative single units, tracking their activity over long timescales.
evidence: This is a primary claim about the authors' methodological contribution, described in the text and detailed in subsequent sections.

claim: The authors' spike-sorting algorithm surpassed the performance of spike-sorting methods that assume stationarity of spike waveforms on ground-truth datasets.
source: We validated our algorithm on ground-truth datasets and found that it surpassed the performance of spike-sorting methods that assume stationarity of spike waveforms.
evidence: This claim is supported by validation experiments described in the manuscript and shown in Figure 3.

claim: The authors recorded from motor cortex and striatum continuously over several months.
source: We used this integrated system to record from motor cortex and striatum continuously over several months
evidence: This is a primary experimental claim supported by data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Months-long recordings revealed remarkable stability in basic neuronal properties such as firing rates and inter-spike interval distributions.
source: Months-long recordings from motor cortex and striatum made and analyzed with our system revealed remarkable stability in basic neuronal properties, such as firing rates and inter-spike interval distributions.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data presented in Figure 5.

claim: Interneuronal correlations were stable over several weeks.
source: Interneuronal correlations and the representation of different movements and behaviors were similarly stable.
evidence: This finding is supported by data presented in Figure 6.

claim: The representation of different movements and behaviors was stable over several weeks.
source: Interneuronal correlations and the representation of different movements and behaviors were similarly stable.
evidence: This finding is supported by data presented in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: The authors' experimental platform enables fully automated long-term continuous extracellular recordings from large numbers of neurons in freely behaving rodents.
source: To address this, we designed and deployed a modular and low-cost recording system that enables fully automated long-term continuous extracellular recordings from large numbers of neurons in freely behaving rodents engaged in natural behaviors and prescribed tasks.
evidence: This is a primary methodological claim supported by the description of the system in Figure 1 and subsequent experimental results.

claim: The animal's home-cage doubles as the experimental chamber in the ARTS system.
source: In ARTS, the animal's home-cage doubles as the experimental chamber, making it a suitable platform for continuous long-term recordings.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental setup supported by citation to prior work (Poddar et al., 2013).

claim: The tethering system connects the implanted recording device via a cable to a passive commutator attached to a carriage that rides on a low-friction linear slide.
source: Our solution connects the implanted recording device via a cable to a passive commutator (Sutton and Miller, 1963) attached to a carriage that rides on a low-friction linear slide.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental apparatus shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The carriage is counterweighted by a pulley, resulting in a small constant upwards force (<10 g) on the cable.
source: The carriage is counterweighted by a pulley, resulting in a small constant upwards force (<10 g) on the cable that keeps it taut and out of the animal's reach without unduly affecting its movements.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental apparatus with a specific measurement.

claim: Extracellular signals are recorded from 16 implanted tetrodes at 30 kHz sampling rate.
source: Extracellular signals recorded in behaving animals from 16 implanted tetrodes at 30 kHz sampling rate are amplified and digitized on a custom-designed head-stage
evidence: This is a description of the recording parameters of the experimental system.

claim: The head-stage features a 3-axis accelerometer that measures head movements at high temporal resolution.
source: To characterize the behavior of animals throughout the recordings, the head-stage features a 3-axis accelerometer that measures head movements at high temporal resolution (Venkatraman et al., 2010) (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental apparatus supported by citation and shown in Figure 1.

claim: The large volumes of behavioral and neural data amount to approximately 0.5 TB/day/rat.
source: The large volumes of behavioral and neural data (~0.5 TB/day/rat) are streamed to custom-built high-capacity servers
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement of data volume from the experimental system.

claim: Automated spike-sorting methods face three major challenges: capturing activity of neurons with widely varying firing rates, contending with changing spike shapes over time, and processing very large numbers of spikes efficiently.
source: These face three major challenges (Rey et al., 2015a). First, they must reliably capture the activity of simultaneously recorded neurons whose firing rates can vary over many orders of magnitude (Hromádka et al., 2008; Mizuseki and Buzsáki, 2013). Second, they have to contend with spike shapes from recorded units changing significantly over time (Figure 1C) (Dickey et al., 2009; Emondi et al., 2004; Fraser and Schwartz, 2012). This can lead to sorting errors such as incorrect splitting of a single unit's spikes into multiple clusters, or incorrect merging of spikes from multiple units in the same cluster (Figure 1D). Third, automated methods must be capable of processing very large numbers of spikes in a reliable and efficient manner
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and illustrated in Figure 1C-D.

claim: In the authors' experience, continuous recordings generate over 10^10 spikes per rat over 3 months for 64 channel recordings.
source: (in our experience, >1010 spikes per rat over a time span of 3 months for 64 channel recordings).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the authors' experimental data.

claim: FAST comprises two main steps: local clustering to create de-noised representations of spiking events, and chaining together de-noised spikes using an integer linear programming algorithm.
source: Our Fast Automated Spike Tracker (FAST) (Poddar et al., 2017) comprises two main steps (Figure 2). First, to compress the datasets and normalize for large variations in firing rates between units, it applies 'local clustering' to create de-noised representations of spiking events in the data (Figure 2A–C). In a second step, FAST chains together de-noised spikes belonging to the same putative single unit over time using an integer linear programming algorithm (Figure 2D) (Vazquez-Reina et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a description of the algorithm methodology shown in Figure 2.

claim: FAST runs two to three times faster than the rate at which data is acquired (for 64 electrodes).
source: FAST is an efficient and modular data processing pipeline that, depending on overall spike rates, runs two to three times faster on our custom built storage servers (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) than the rate at which the data (64 electrodes) is acquired.
evidence: This is a quantitative performance measurement of the algorithm.

claim: FAST could, in principle, be used for online sorting.
source: This implies that FAST could, in principle, also be used for online sorting, although we are currently running it offline.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential applications of the algorithm based on its performance characteristics.

claim: FAST performed as well as BEER on relatively short (4-6 min long) recordings from paired intracellular-extracellular datasets.
source: We found that FAST performed as well as BEER on these relatively short (4–6 min long) recordings (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, n = 5 recordings).
evidence: This is a finding from validation experiments shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The performance of FAST significantly outperformed BEER when recordings spanned days in synthetic datasets.
source: In contrast, the performance of FAST, which was comparable to BEER for short recording durations, significantly outperformed it when the recordings spanned days (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a finding from validation experiments on synthetic data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: FAST performed better than BEER over recording durations longer than 64 hr for single electrode recording configurations.
source: FAST was also found to perform better than BEER over recording durations longer than 64 hr for single electrode recording configurations that are commonly used in non-human primates (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from validation experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The authors implanted tetrode drives (16 tetrodes, 64 channels) into dorsolateral striatum (n=2) or motor cortex (n=3) of Long Evans rats.
source: To demonstrate the utility of our experimental platform and analysis pipeline for long-term neural recordings, we implanted tetrode drives (16 tetrodes, 64 channels) into dorsolateral striatum (n = 2) or motor cortex (n = 3) of Long Evans rats (Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedures.

claim: The authors recorded electrophysiological and behavioral data continuously for more than 3 months.
source: We recorded electrophysiological and behavioral data continuously (Figure 4A), with only brief interruptions, for more than 3 months.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental duration supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The recordings terminated not because of technical issues but because the experiments reached their end points.
source: We note that our recordings terminated not because of technical issues with the implant or recording apparatus, but because we deemed the experiments to have reached their end points.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental design and termination criteria.

claim: The authors isolated a total of 1550 units from motor cortex and 1477 units from striatum using FAST.
source: We used our automated spike-sorting method (FAST) to cluster spike waveforms into putative single units, isolating a total of 1550 units from motor cortex and 1477 units from striatum (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from applying FAST to the experimental data.

claim: On average, single units could be tracked over 3.2 days for motor cortex and 7.4 days for striatum.
source: On average, we could track single units over several days (mean: 3.2 days for motor cortex and 7.4 days for striatum)
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement of unit tracking duration from the experimental data.

claim: 11% of motor cortex units and 36% of striatum units were tracked continuously for more than a week.
source: with significant fractions of units tracked continuously for more than a week (11% and 36% in motor cortex and striatum, respectively)
evidence: This is a quantitative result shown in Figure 4B.

claim: 0.4% of motor cortex units and 1.7% of striatum units were tracked for more than a month.
source: and even a month (0.4% in motor cortex and 1.7% in striatum, Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result shown in Figure 4B.

claim: On average, 19 ± 15 units were recorded simultaneously in motor cortex and 41 ± 20 units in striatum.
source: On average, we recorded simultaneously from 19 ± 15 units in motor cortex and 41 ± 20 units in striatum (mean ± standard deviation) (two example rats shown in Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: 61.4% of motor cortical units and 64.6% of striatal units satisfied conservative cluster quality criteria.
source: Assessing the mean cluster quality of the units over their recording lifetimes, we found that 61.4% of motor cortical (n = 952) and 64.6% of striatal units (n = 954) satisfied our conservative criteria (Quirk et al., 2009; Schmitzer-Torbert et al., 2005; Sigurdsson et al., 2010) (Isolation distance >= 25, L-ratio <= 0.3 and fraction of ISIs below 2 ms <= 1%).
evidence: This is a quantitative assessment of cluster quality from the experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: 83.7% of motor cortical units and 93.2% of striatal units met quality criteria for at least one hour of recording.
source: However, 83.7% of motor cortical units (n = 1298) and 93.2% of striatal units (n = 1376) met these criteria for at least one hour of recording.
evidence: This is a quantitative assessment of cluster quality from the experimental data.

claim: The average signal-to-noise ratio of units isolated from DLS was 15.4 ± 7.4 and from MC was 14.5 ± 7.2.
source: The average signal-to-noise ratio of units isolated from the DLS and MC was found to be 15.4 ± 7.4 and 14.5 ± 7.2, respectively (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Discontinuous tracking over day-long gaps was found to be highly error-prone in the authors' dataset.
source: In our data set, we found discontinuous tracking over day-long gaps to be highly error-prone (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The authors clustered motor cortical and striatal units into putative principal neurons and interneurons based on spike shapes and firing rates, identifying 366 fast spiking and 1111 medium spiny neurons in striatum, and 686 fast spiking and 864 regular spiking neurons in motor cortex.
source: We clustered motor cortical and striatal units into putative principal neurons and interneurons based on their spike shapes and firing rates (Barthó et al., 2004; Berke et al., 2004; Connors and Gutnick, 1990), thus identifying 366 fast spiking and 1111 medium spiny neurons in striatum, and 686 fast spiking and 864 regular spiking neurons in motor cortex (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a result from cell-type classification shown in Figure 5A, supported by citations to prior classification methods.

claim: Average firing rates appeared log-normally distributed and varied over more than three orders of magnitude (from 0.029 Hz to 40.2 Hz in striatum, and 0.031 Hz to 44.8 Hz in motor cortex).
source: Consistent with previous reports (Hromádka et al., 2008; Mizuseki and Buzsáki, 2013), average firing rates appeared log-normally distributed and varied over more than three orders of magnitude (from 0.029 Hz to 40.2 Hz in striatum, and 0.031 Hz to 44.8 Hz in motor cortex; Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data shown in Figure 5A, consistent with prior reports.

claim: Average firing rates remained largely unchanged even over 20 days of recording.
source: Average firing rates remained largely unchanged even over 20 days of recording (Figure 5B–D)
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 5B-D.

claim: Activity levels of single units in both cortex and striatum are stable over long timescales, and individual units maintain their own firing rate set-point.
source: suggesting that activity levels of single units in both cortex and striatum are stable over long timescales, and that individual units maintain their own firing rate set-point (Hengen et al., 2016; Marder and Goaillard, 2006).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the firing rate stability data, supported by citations to prior work on homeostatic mechanisms.

claim: The inter-spike interval distribution of single units remained largely unchanged across days.
source: Similar to firing rate, we found that the ISI distribution of single units remained largely unchanged across days (Figure 5E–F).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 5E-F.

claim: 21.1% of striatal pairs and 37.6% of motor cortex pairs were significantly correlated.
source: We found that 21.1% of striatal pairs (n = 18697 pairs) and 37.6% motor cortex pairs (n = 9235 pairs) were significantly correlated (Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from cross-correlogram analysis.

claim: The average absolute time-lag of significantly correlated pairs was 13.0 ± 26.3 ms (median: 4 ms) for striatum and 23.9 ± 28.8 ms (median: 13.0 ms) for motor cortex.
source: The average absolute time-lag of significantly correlated pairs was 13.0 ± 26.3 ms (median: 4 ms) and 23.9 ± 28.8 ms (median: 13.0 ms) for striatum and motor cortex respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from cross-correlogram analysis.

claim: Pairwise spike correlations were remarkably stable, remaining essentially unchanged even after 10 days.
source: The pairwise spike correlations were remarkably stable, remaining essentially unchanged even after 10 days (Figure 6B–C), consistent with a very stable underlying network (Grutzendler et al., 2002; Yang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 6B-C and consistent with prior work on structural stability.

claim: The authors developed an algorithm for automatically classifying a rat's behavior into 'states' using high-resolution measurements of head acceleration and local field potentials.
source: To do this, we developed an algorithm for automatically classifying a rat's behavior into 'states' using high-resolution measurements of head acceleration and local field potentials (LFPs).
evidence: This is a methodological claim about behavioral classification.

claim: The behavioral classification method distinguishes repetitive behaviors, eating, active exploration, task engagement, quiet wakefulness, rapid eye movement, and slow wave sleep, and assigns approximately 88% of recording time to one of these states.
source: Our method distinguishes repetitive behaviors (such as grooming), eating, active exploration, task engagement as well as quiet wakefulness, rapid eye movement, and slow wave sleep (Gervasoni et al., 2004; Venkatraman et al., 2010) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1, Materials and methods), and assigns ~88% of the recording time to one of these states.
evidence: This is a description of the behavioral classification method and its performance, supported by citations.

claim: Firing rates of both striatal and motor cortical units depended on what the animal was doing.
source: Not surprisingly, we found that firing rates of both striatal and motor cortical units depended on what the animal was doing (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a finding from behavioral state analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The relative firing rates in different behavioral states (i.e. a cell's 'state tuning') remained stable over several weeks-long timescales.
source: Interestingly, the relative firing rates in different behavioral states (i.e. a cell's 'state tuning') remained stable over several weeks-long timescales (Figure 7A–B), even as they varied substantially between different neurons (Figure 7A,C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 7A-C.

claim: Interneuronal spike correlations were modulated by behavioral state, and this dependence was stable over time.
source: Additionally, we observed that interneuronal spike correlations were also modulated by behavioral state (Figure 7D), and this dependence was also stable over time (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 7D-E.

claim: The percentage of units with significant response fields during repetitive behavior, exploration, and eating was 19.7%, 9.5%, and 18.4% respectively for striatum, and 18.7%, 7.6%, and 22.5% for motor cortex.
source: The percentage of units with significant response fields during repetitive behavior, exploration, and eating was 19.7% (n = 291), 9.5% (n = 140) and 18.4% (n = 272), respectively, for the striatum, and 18.7% (n = 290), 7.6% (n = 118) and 22.5% (n = 349) for the motor cortex.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from spike-triggered average analysis.

claim: Movement STAs varied substantially between neurons and across behavioral states, but were stable for the same unit when compared over at least 20 days, within a particular state.
source: Movement STAs varied substantially between neurons and across behavioral states, but were stable for the same unit when compared over at least 20 days, within a particular state (Figure 8A–B).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 8A-B.

claim: The fraction of units whose activity was significantly locked to lever-press or nose-poke was 22.2% and 23.2% in striatum, and 12.3% and 18.7% in motor cortex.
source: The fraction of units whose activity was significantly locked to the lever-press or nose-poke (see Materials and methods) was 22.2% (n = 328) and 23.2% (n = 343) in striatum, and 12.3% (n = 190) and 18.7% (n = 290) in motor cortex (Figure 8C), respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from PETH analysis shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The times of peak firing in PETHs were distributed over a range of delays relative to the time of behavioral events.
source: When comparing PETHs of different units for the same behavioral events, we observed that the times of peak firing were distributed over a range of delays relative to the time of the events (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is an observation from PETH analysis shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The PETHs of individual units were remarkably similar when compared across days.
source: However, despite the heterogeneity in PETHs across the population of units, the PETHs of individual units were remarkably similar when compared across days (Figure 8D–F).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 8D-F.

claim: The vast majority (between 88% and 98%) of recorded units were stable based on regression analysis of similarity metrics.
source: The distribution of stability indices was unimodal and centered at 0 day−1 for every similarity metric, indicating that the vast majority (between 88% and 98%) of recorded units were stable (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B, Table 2) given a conservative threshold (slope >= -0.025 day−1 and p>=0.05).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from stability analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B and Table 2.

claim: A small fraction (~2-12%) of recorded units were relatively less stable over longer timescales.
source: Interestingly, a negative skew was also apparent in these distributions implying that a small fraction (~2–12%) of our recorded units were relatively less stable over longer timescales (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B, Table 2)
evidence: This is a finding from stability analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B and Table 2.

claim: No unit was found to have a stability index lower than -0.1 day^-1.
source: however no unit was found to have a stability index lower than -0.1 day−1.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from stability analysis.

claim: Automating the recording process eliminates manual steps that are time-consuming and can be detrimental to recordings and stressful for animals.
source: First, it eliminates the manual steps of intermittent recordings, such as transferring animals to and from their recording chambers, plugging and unplugging recording cables etc., which, besides being time-consuming, can be detrimental to the recordings (Buzsáki et al., 2015) and stressful for the animals (Dobrakovová and Jurcovicová, 1984; Longordo et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a claim about the benefits of automation supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The automated system should enable a single researcher to supervise tens, if not hundreds, of recordings simultaneously.
source: Indeed, our system should enable a single researcher to supervise tens, if not hundreds, of recordings simultaneously, thus radically improving the ease and throughput with which such experiments can be performed.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the scalability of the system.

claim: State-of-the-art methods for processing extracellular recordings require significant human input and make analysis of large datasets prohibitively time-consuming.
source: This is in large part because state-of-the-art methods for processing extracellular recordings require significant human input and hence make the analysis of large datasets prohibitively time-consuming (Hengen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a claim about limitations of existing methods supported by citation.

claim: FAST overcomes the bottleneck of manual analysis, dramatically increasing the feasibility of continuous and high-throughput long-term recordings.
source: Our fast automated spike tracking (FAST) algorithm overcomes this bottleneck, thereby dramatically increasing the feasibility of continuous and high-throughput long-term recordings of extracellular signals in behaving animals.
evidence: This is a claim about the impact of FAST based on its performance characteristics.

claim: Calcium indicators function as chelators of free calcium ions and could interfere with calcium-dependent plasticity processes and compromise cell health over the long-term.
source: Furthermore, calcium indicators function as chelators of free calcium ions (Hires et al., 2008; Tsien, 1980) and could interfere with calcium-dependent plasticity processes (Zucker, 1999) and, over the long-term, compromise the health of cells (Looger and Griesbeck, 2012).
evidence: This is a claim about potential issues with calcium imaging supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Discrepancies in calcium imaging studies may have been contributed to by variables such as photobleaching, phototoxicity, and interference with cellular processes.
source: These variables may have contributed to discrepancies in studies using longitudinal calcium imaging, with many reporting dramatic day-to-day fluctuations in neural activity patterns (Driscoll et al., 2017; Huber et al., 2012; Liberti et al., 2016; Ziv et al., 2013) while some others report more stable representations (Peters et al., 2014; Rose et al., 2016), leaving open the question of how stable the brain really is (Clopath et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential causes of discrepancies in prior studies.

claim: Intermittent electrical recordings may fail to reliably track the same neurons over multiple days.
source: While electrical measurements of spiking activity do not suffer from the same drawbacks, intermittent recordings may fail to reliably track the same neurons over multiple days (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–E) (Dickey et al., 2009; Emondi et al., 2004; Fraser and Schwartz, 2012; Tolias et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D-E and citations to prior work.

claim: Contrasting findings about neural stability in prior studies could be due to systematic errors in unit tracking across discontinuous recording sessions.
source: Such contrasting findings could be due to systematic errors in unit tracking across discontinuous recording sessions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), or the choice of statistical framework used to assess stability (Rokni et al., 2007; Stevenson et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential sources of error in prior studies, supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and citations.

claim: The use of activity metrics to track units may bias datasets towards subsets of units whose spike waveforms and neural dynamics do not change with time.
source: Complications may also arise from the use of activity metrics, such as firing rate and ISI distributions, to track units in many studies (Dickey et al., 2009; Emondi et al., 2004; Fraser and Schwartz, 2012; Ganguly and Carmena, 2009; Greenberg and Wilson, 2004; Jackson and Fetz, 2007; McMahon et al., 2014a; Okun et al., 2016; Thompson and Best, 1990; Tolias et al., 2007), which may bias datasets towards subsets of units whose spike waveforms (Figure 1C–D) and neural dynamics (Figure 8—figure supplement 1) do not change with time.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential biases in prior studies, supported by data in Figures 1C-D and 8—figure supplement 1, and citations.

claim: The authors' continuous recordings suggest remarkable stability in spiking statistics, neuronal interactions, and tuning properties of the majority of motor cortical and striatal units.
source: Our continuous recordings, which allow for the reliable characterization of single neuron properties over long time periods, suggest a remarkable stability in both spiking statistics (Figure 5), neuronal interactions (Figure 6), and tuning properties (Figures 7 and 8) of the majority of motor cortical and striatal units.
evidence: This is a summary claim about the primary findings, supported by data in Figures 5-8.

claim: The findings support the view that motor cortical and striatal neural networks are highly stable systems in terms of their dynamics and connectivity.
source: Taken together with studies showing long-term structural stability at the level of synapses (Grutzendler et al., 2002; Yang et al., 2009), our findings support the view that these neural networks are, overall, highly stable systems, both in terms of their dynamics and connectivity.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on the authors' findings and prior work on structural stability.

claim: Discrepancies between the authors' findings and other studies reporting instability could be due to inherent differences between brain areas.
source: Discrepancies between our findings and other studies that report long-term instability of neural activity could, in some cases, be due to inherent differences between brain areas.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential explanations for differences with prior studies.

claim: Neural dynamics of circuits involved in transient information storage or flexible sensorimotor associations may be intrinsically more unstable than circuits responsible for sensory processing or motor control.
source: Neural dynamics of circuits involved in transient information storage such as the hippocampus (Mankin et al., 2012; Ziv et al., 2013), and flexible sensorimotor associations such as the parietal cortex (Morcos and Harvey, 2016) may be intrinsically more unstable than circuits responsible for sensory processing or motor control (Ganguly and Carmena, 2009; McMahon et al., 2014b; Peters et al., 2014; Rose et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative claim about functional differences between brain areas, supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Recent studies have found higher synaptic turnover in the hippocampus compared to primary sensory and motor cortices.
source: In line with this hypothesis, recent studies have found higher synaptic turnover in the hippocampus (Attardo et al., 2015) in comparison to primary sensory and motor cortices (Holtmaat et al., 2005; Xu et al., 2009; Yang et al., 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies on synaptic turnover.

claim: It is not clear whether structural plasticity functions to destabilize or stabilize neural activity.
source: although it is not clear whether structural plasticity functions to destabilize or stabilize neural activity (Clopath et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a statement about uncertainty in the field, supported by citation.

claim: The authors hypothesize that neural activity would be far more variable when an animal is learning a task or motor skill.
source: We hypothesize that neural activity would be far more variable when an animal is learning a task or motor skill (Kawai et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about neural dynamics during learning, supported by citation.

claim: The experimental platform makes it feasible to characterize learning-related changes in task representations and relate them to reorganization of network dynamics over long time-scales.
source: Our experimental platform makes it feasible to characterize learning-related changes in task representations and relate them to reorganization of network dynamics over long time-scales.
evidence: This is a claim about the capabilities of the experimental platform for future studies.

claim: The modular and flexible experimental platform can easily incorporate innovations in recording technology.
source: Our modular and flexible experimental platform can easily incorporate such innovations.
evidence: This is a claim about the adaptability of the experimental platform.

claim: FAST solves a major bottleneck by allowing increasingly large datasets to be efficiently parsed.
source: Importantly, our novel and automated analysis pipeline (FAST) solves a major bottleneck downstream of these solutions by allowing increasingly large datasets to be efficiently parsed, thus making automated recording and analysis of large populations of neurons in behaving animals a feasible prospect.
evidence: This is a summary claim about the impact of FAST based on its performance.

claim: Rats were trained twice daily on a timed lever-pressing task before implantation.
source: Before implantation, rats were trained twice daily on a timed lever-pressing task (Kawai et al., 2015) using our fully automated home-cage training system (Poddar et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedures.

claim: After 7 days of recovery from surgery, rats were returned to their home-cages outfitted with an electrophysiology recording extension.
source: After 7 days of recovery, rats were returned to their home-cages, which had been outfitted with an electrophysiology recording extension (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedures.

claim: Neural and behavioral data was recorded continuously for 12-16 weeks with only brief interruptions (median time of 0.2 hr).
source: Neural and behavioral data was recorded continuously for 12–16 weeks with only brief interruptions (median time of 0.2 hr) for occasional troubleshooting.
evidence: This is a description of the recording duration and continuity.

claim: The accelerometer output was sampled at 7.5 kHz per axis.
source: The output of the accelerometer was sampled at 7.5 kHz per axis.
evidence: This is a technical specification of the recording system.

claim: Continuous video was recorded at 30 frames per second.
source: We also recorded 24/7 continuous video at 30 frames per second with a CCD camera (Flea 3, Point Grey) or a webcam (Agama V-1325R).
evidence: This is a technical specification of the recording system.

claim: Tetrodes were electroplated to lower electrode impedances to approximately 100-150 kΩ.
source: The wires were electroplated in a gold (5355, SIFCO) and 0.1% carbon nanotubes (Cheap Tubes dispersed MWNTs, 95wt% <8 nm) solution with 0.1% polyvinylpyrrolidone surfactant (PVP-40, Sigma-Aldrich) to lower electrode impedances to ~100–150 kΩ (Ferguson et al., 2009; Keefer et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a description of the electrode preparation procedure with target impedance values.

claim: The custom-designed head-stage weighs less than four grams and measures 18 mm x 28 mm in size.
source: Our lightweight, low-noise and low-cost system for multi-channel extra-cellular electrophysiology (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) uses a 64-channel custom-designed head-stage (made of 2 RHD2132 ICs from Intan Technologies), weighs less than four grams and measures 18 mm x 28 mm in size.
evidence: This is a technical specification of the recording hardware.

claim: The head-stage filters, amplifies, and digitizes extracellular neural signals at 16 bits/sample and 30 kHz per second per channel.
source: The head-stage filters, amplifies, and digitizes extracellular neural signals at 16 bits/sample and 30 kHz per second per channel.
evidence: This is a technical specification of the recording hardware.

claim: The parts for a complete 64-channel electrophysiology extension cost less than $1500, excluding the recording computer.
source: The parts for a complete 64-channel electrophysiology extension, including head-stage, FPGA board, commutator, and pulley system, but excluding the recording computer, cost less than $1500.
evidence: This is a cost estimate for the recording system components.

claim: The percent overlap between automated accelerometer-based separation of active/inactive periods and manual scoring was 92.9% for inactive periods and 96.9% for active periods.
source: To verify the accuracy of our accelerometer-based separation of active and inactive behaviors, we calculated the percent overlap between our automated separation with that of a human observer who manually scored active and inactive periods using simultaneously recorded webcam video data (n = 29831 s video from 4 rats).
evidence: This is a validation result comparing automated and manual behavioral classification, shown in a table in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Rats spent most of their time sleeping (44 ± 3%) or resting (6 ± 2%).
source: Consistent with prior studies (Gervasoni et al., 2004), we found that rats spent most of their time sleeping (44 ± 3%) or resting (6 ± 2%) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from behavioral classification, consistent with prior studies.

claim: Sleep occurred more frequently when lights were on (58 ± 7%) versus when they were off (33 ± 9%), consistent with the nocturnal habits of rats.
source: Sleep occurred at all hours, but was more frequent when lights were on (58 ± 7%) versus when they were off (33 ± 9%), consistent with the nocturnal habits of rats (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from behavioral classification shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Using the seizure classification algorithm, 11% of time-bins were classified as seizure (12 ± 2% for DLS-implanted rats and 11 ± 2% for MC-implanted rats).
source: Using this classification, 11% of time-bins were classified as seizure (12 ± 2% for the DLS-implanted rats and 11 ± 2% for the MC-implanted rats) similar to previously published reports (Shaw, 2004).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from seizure detection, consistent with prior reports.

claim: Each storage server has 60 TB of usable space that can be read at approximately 16 gigabits per second.
source: Due to the redundancy, each server has 60 TB of usable space that can be read at approximately 16 gigabits per second (Gbps).
evidence: This is a technical specification of the storage infrastructure.

claim: In the authors' recordings, the mean event detection rate was 62.4 ± 39.0 Hz, resulting in an average duration of 16 s for a 1000 spike block.
source: In our recordings, the mean event detection rate was 62.4 ± 39.0 Hz (mean ± SD, n = 80 tetrode recordings), resulting in an average duration of 16 s for a 1000 spike block.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental data used to characterize FAST's tracking time-scale.

claim: Local clustering in Step 1 of FAST yielded centroids at a rate of 8.0 ± 2.6 per 1000 spike block in the authors' recordings.
source: In our own recordings, local clustering in Step 1 yielded centroids at a rate of 8.0 ± 2.6 per 1000 spike block.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from applying FAST to the experimental data.

claim: The approximate tracking time-scale of FAST in the authors' recordings is 33 minutes.
source: This yields an approximate tracking time-scale of 16*1000/8 = 2000 s or 33 min.
evidence: This is a calculated estimate based on the measured parameters of the recordings.

claim: In the authors' dataset, the number of manual mergers required per unit was, on average, 14.7 ± 30.6, which translated to an average of 1.3 manual chain mergers per tetrode per day.
source: In our dataset, the number of manual mergers required per unit was, on average, 14.7 ± 30.6 (mean ± SD), which translated to an average of 1.3 manual chain mergers per tetrode per day.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement of the manual effort required for chain merging.

claim: Only 2% of all unit chains (or 0.027 chains per tetrode per day) required manual splitting due to mis-sorting.
source: In the event of mis-sorting (only 2% of all unit chains, or 0.027 chains per tetrode per day), we manually split these chains using MClust.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement of the error rate of the automated sorting.

claim: It takes about 8 human hours to perform manual verification of FAST output applied to a 3 month long recording on a single tetrode, or approximately 130 hrs for all 16 tetrodes.
source: In our hands, it takes about 8 human hours to perform manual verification of the automated output of FAST applied to a 3 month long recording on a single tetrode, or approximately 130 hrs to process all 16 tetrodes in our recording array.
evidence: This is a measurement of the time required for manual verification.

claim: Manual verification proceeds at a rate about 5.5 times faster than the rate of data-acquisition.
source: Thus manual verification proceeds at a rate about 5.5 times faster than the rate of data-acquisition, which is nearly twice as fast as the slowest automated step of FAST (Step 1).
evidence: This is a calculated comparison of manual verification speed to data acquisition rate.
